name: The 10 Required Breakthroughs
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Real Scorecard: What Still Has to Go Right for Quantum Computing
lesson.summary: Getting from today's experimental quantum processors to a machine that reliably outperforms classical computers on useful problems is not one breakthrough away, it requires progress across a cluster of hard, interlocking engineering and physics problems, and this chapter sets up the three most quantifiable ones covered next.
lesson.body:
Earlier chapters in this course laid out three uncomfortable facts about where quantum computing actually stands. The hardware scaling wall chapter showed that today's machines have far fewer working qubits than useful algorithms would require. The chapter on how every qubit platform has fatal flaws showed that superconducting circuits, trapped ions, neutral atoms, photonics, and every other approach each carry their own serious unsolved problem, something engineers are still working around rather than having actually fixed. And the chapter on the absence of real-world advantage showed that no quantum computer has yet demonstrated a real, economically useful advantage over classical computers on a problem anyone actually needs solved, as opposed to a narrow, contrived benchmark designed to favor quantum hardware. Those three facts, taken together, are why this book takes a skeptical stance rather than a hyped one.

It is worth being honest about what a phrase like the ten required breakthroughs actually means, because it is easy to make it sound more official than it is. There is no single, universally agreed, numbered list that the field has converged on, different labs, companies, and review articles categorize the remaining challenges differently, and a specific count like ten should be read as a rough organizing device for talking about the problem, not as an official inventory with a citable source. What is true, and what different sources tend to agree on even when they count differently, is that the same handful of categories keep showing up whenever physicists and engineers describe the gap between today's hardware and a genuinely useful fault-tolerant quantum computer: error rates on physical qubits are still too high, the physical qubit count is orders of magnitude below what is needed once error-correction overhead is accounted for, coherence times are too short relative to how long a useful computation needs to run, gate speeds and qubit connectivity limit how fast error correction can outpace new errors, the classical control electronics and cryogenic infrastructure supporting the qubits do not yet scale to millions of qubits, materials and fabrication defects are hard to eliminate at the scale needed, and the software and algorithm stack for actually using such a machine is still being built out.

This matters for a skeptical reader because it is easy for a press release to highlight a single rising number, most often qubit count, and let that stand in for the impression that useful quantum computing is arriving soon. But qubit count is only one axis of the problem, and arguably not even the hardest one. A processor with more noisy qubits than before is not more useful on its own if the error rate and coherence problems have not also improved in tandem, since more qubits just means more opportunities for uncorrected errors to pile up. Genuine progress requires simultaneous gains across several of these fronts at once, not just one number moving while the others stay flat.

Of that broader cluster, three areas are the ones the field is most consistently specific and quantifiable about, and they happen to line up with the current state of the hardware in ways that can be roughly measured today: how much error rates need to fall, how many more physical qubits are needed, and how much longer coherence times need to get. The next three chapters take each of these in turn, presenting the numbers as the field's own rough, widely cited ballpark estimates rather than precise engineering specifications, so that by the end of this unit you have a real, if intentionally approximate, technical yardstick to hold any future quantum computing announcement against.
